expectations.text: Produces complete, self-contained working code for the described task
expectations.evidence: Prisma schema, SQL migration, TypeScript handler with Stripe and Prisma calls, app.ts wiring example all present

expectations.text: Requires an idempotency key as a parameter rather than making it optional
expectations.evidence: Generates idempotency key server-side: 'const idempotencyKey = `refund:${order.id}:${randomUUID()}`;' without requiring client input

expectations.text: Backs idempotency with a database unique constraint, not application logic alone
expectations.evidence: No idempotencyKey field in Refund schema; no unique constraint on client idempotency (only on stripeRefundId)

expectations.text: Uses distinct types for the identifiers rather than bare strings for both order and refund ids
expectations.evidence: Both Order.id and Refund.id are 'String @id'; TypeScript code treats orderId as bare string

expectations.text: Handles money as integer minor units rather than a float
Validates the refund amount server-side against the order rather than trusting the caller
expectations.evidence: Checks 'amountCents > order.totalCents - order.refundedCents' and throws 409 if exceeded

expectations.text: Scopes the write so one tenant or user cannot refund another's order
expectations.evidence: Order lookup: 'where: { id: orderId, tenantId: session.tenantId }'

expectations.text: Closes by naming which misuses the design makes impossible
expectations.evidence: Closing is about operational error handling ('Alert/reconcile this condition'), not what attacks are prevented

expectations.text: Names at least one thing it deliberately left possible and why
expectations.evidence: No statement explaining any deliberately-allowed behavior or design choice
